extracted.intended_audience: readers of the Public Advertiser; politically engaged British public (late 18th century)
extracted.subtask_description: A political-opinion letter assessing the proper behaviour and duties of the sovereign, ministers, and Parliament; it lays out normative standards for constitutional government and public conduct. The document argues what is proper or improper in executive and legislative action, and what remedies or responsibilities follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign's public demeanour
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign should never appear but in an amiable light to his subjects; it has not been usual in this country to see the sovereign personally at variance or engage in a direct altercation with his subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts of grace and indulgence are wisely appropriated to him and should be constantly performed by himself. In a limited monarchy no man should leave the royal presence discontented; the king should be beloved rather than feared. Anti-pattern: the king answering absolutely for himself in harsh language (as in France) which breeds fear rather than affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve royal interposition as last resource
rubrics_metrics.description: The interposition of the royal personage should be reserved as the last resource of government; it should not be applied to every ordinary occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ministers' weakness that forces the king to appear on ordinary occasions renders the royal authority cheap and common in the people's opinion, prostituting and dishonouring the sacred character of the crown. Guidance: use royal presence only for important, well-considered occasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministerial responsibility for severe measures
rubrics_metrics.description: When measures of greater severity are necessary, the minister who advises them should take the execution and odium of them entirely upon himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A minister who forces the sovereign to speak harshly but then fails to support or punish those responsible betrays his master and violates the spirit of the constitution. Anti-pattern: advising harsh royal language but leaving the king exposed and unsupported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firmness of government = consistent ministerial policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Firmness of government means an uniform system of measures, deliberately adopted and resolutely maintained by the servants of the crown; not a peevish asperity in the language and behaviour of the sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A weak, irresolute monarch may preside over wise government; conversely, a capricious prince can render government feeble and inconsistent. Evaluate government firmness by its consistent policies and ministerial steadiness rather than the sovereign's tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public measures' reputation rests with ministers, not the king
rubrics_metrics.description: The reputation of public measures depends upon the minister, who is responsible; not upon the king, whose private opinions are not supposed to have any weight against the advice of his council.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sovereign's personal authority should never be interposed in public affairs; ministers should accept credit or blame for public measures. Anti-pattern: ministers persuading the king to act publicly and then failing to back or enforce those acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers must not expose the sovereign to personal hatred or contempt
rubrics_metrics.description: A minister betrays his master and violates constitutional spirit when he exposes the chief magistrate to the personal hatred or contempt of his subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ministers should execute unpopular or severe policies themselves and shield the sovereign from personal vilification. Example of harm: a king placed alone on the public stage to bear ridicule and odium because ministers will not undertake enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary prudence and responsiveness to constituents
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of Parliament should consider the known disposition of their constituents and, without dishonour to their firmness, retract an opinion too hastily adopted when they see its alarm and general public opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prudence requires attention to public sentiment; ministers and Parliament would secure their own interest by concessions satisfactory to the moderate part of the people. Anti-pattern: persisting in measures despite strong national opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliament must follow law and internal rules; avoid supporting illegal decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: To support a former illegal and unjust decision, the house was obliged to violate some of the best known and established rules of the house (e.g., declaring it not the rule to divide a complicated question at a member's request).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A legitimate decision cannot be built on continued falsehood and injustice; breaking procedural rules to sustain prior errors undermines the assembly's integrity. Example: speaker's pretended ignorance and eventual decision for ministry blamed as baseness.

rubrics_metrics.name: House of Lords should preserve constitutional checks
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Lords must not surrender its constitutional check and reciprocal control over the House of Commons (for example, by resolving they had no right to impeach a Commons judgment in any case), because such surrender removes a crucial protection of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By giving up their right of oversight, the Lords silence themselves and cannot interpose to protect subjects or defend laws; such concessions likely come with compensations paid at the people's expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: People as ultimate constitutional recourse
rubrics_metrics.description: When other resources fail, the last argument of the people will often carry more than persuasion to Parliament or supplication to the throne.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The people performed their part with dignity, spirit, and perseverance; their voice is intelligible and expressive and may compel action when legal or parliamentary means are obstructed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers should act decisively in fiscal policy, not piecemeal
rubrics_metrics.description: A great operation directed to an important object, though it fail, marks the genius and elevates a minister's character; a poor contracted understanding deals in little schemes which dishonour him if they fail and do him no credit when they succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Lord North's attempt to reduce the four-per-cents by tampering piecemeal warned holders and raised price, making the plan counterproductive. Guidance: employ decisive, proportionate measures rather than gradual tampering that advantages holders against the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliament must address colonial grievances substantively
rubrics_metrics.description: In repealing offensive acts the Parliament has done everything but remove the offence; they relinquished the revenue but preserved the contention (e.g., continuation of the tea-duty as an odious, unprofitable assertion of right).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superficial concession that leaves the principle contested fails to resolve the grievance. Parliament should remove both the revenue and the contested principle to heal relations with colonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers are public servants, not private domestics of the sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministers are no longer the public servants of the state, but the private domestics of the sovereign when they permit a particular class to call themselves the king's friends as if the body of the people were the king's enemies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government must serve the public interest rather than circle the monarch with a small faction of favourites; relying on a narrow party as the king's consolation alienates the people and risks repeating the errors of past monarchs who trusted only a few intimate favourites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative assemblies must not prefer infamy to danger
rubrics_metrics.description: A House of Commons conscious of its motives may prefer infamy to danger by tolerating acts contrary to their duty (e.g., failing to expel refractory members after provocation), thus forfeiting credit and dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemblies should enforce their rules and expel members who defy constitutional practice rather than tamely submit and thereby enable dangerous precedents. Example: allowing certain members to remain prevented testing a doctrine of incapacitation fairly.
